paper.central_claim: MetaAgent: starting from a minimal reason-plus-help-seeking workflow with a tool router, an agent that after each task distills self-reflection and ground-truth-verified reflection into a concise experience text carried into later contexts, and builds an in-house persistent knowledge base from its tool-use history ('meta tool learning', no parameter updates), outperforms workflow-based baselines and matches or exceeds end-to-end trained agents on GAIA, WebWalkerQA and BrowseComp.

evidence.quote:
To bridge the gap between novice and expert tool use, MetaAgent conducts self reflection and verified reflection after each task, distilling actionable experience into concise texts. These are dynamically incorporated into future input sequences
𝒳
{\mathcal{X}}
, allowing MetaAgent to continually refine its task planning and tool-use strategies. Meanwhile, MetaAgent organizes its interaction history with the tool router
Γ

, gradually building an in-house tool that manages accumulated external knowledge in a persistent memory. As MetaAgent interacts with external tools over time, this in-house tool becomes increasingly informative, enabling more effective retrieval and integration of relevant knowledge for future tasks.

We refer to this continual process of learning from both experience and tool use as
meta tool learning
. Through meta tool learning, MetaAgent evolves autonomously, incrementally improving its task planning and tool-use strategies without changing model parameters—empowering robust, data-driven adaptation across diverse knowledge discovery scenarios.

In our main experiments, MetaAgent employs QwQ-32B as the central reasoning agent. For web search, we use Google’s
Custom Search JSON API

evidence.quote:
We conduct an ablation study to assess the effectiveness of MetaAgent’s modular design. Specifically, we evaluate five ablated variants: (1) removing self reflection (w/o self reflection); (2) removing verified reflection (w/o verified reflection); (3) removing the use of in-house tools (w/o in-house tool); (4) using only the minimal workflow and (5) replacing the tool router agent with direct in-context tool descriptions (w/ tool description). The results are shown in Figure
3
, which demonstrate that the full MetaAgent design enables clear progression from novice to expert behavior. Notably, the minimal workflow alone performs poorly and can hardly match expert-designed workflow Search-o1, as it only provides basic planning and help-seeking. Our main findings are as follows: (1) both self-reflection and verified reflection are critical, and their combination forms a meta tool learning loop that substantially boosts performance; (2) the in-house tool is essential for providing a global, persistent view of task knowledge, greatly mitigating information loss from single-pass search-and-refine approaches; and (3) substituting the tool router agent with in-context tool descriptions can yield better results than the minimal workflow, as it makes tool usage more explicit for the central agent—but this approach lacks the autonomous, continually evolving capabilities that distinguish MetaAgent’s design.

Figure 3:
Ablation Study. Key components of MetaAgent are individually removed and evaluated on the GAIA benchmark.

evidence.quote:
To further demonstrate MetaAgent’s flexibility and backbone-agnostic design, we substitute its central agent from QwQ-32B to Google’s Gemini-2.5-Flash API and evaluate its performance on the GAIA benchmark. As shown in Table
2
, MetaAgent substantially boosts the deep knowledge discovery capabilities of both open-source and commercial LLMs, consistently outperforming their vanilla counterparts by a wide margin; this improvement is particularly notable when paired with Gemini-2.5-Flash, where MetaAgent’s self-evolving meta tool learning and dynamic context engineering unlock stronger generalization and adaptive tool-use strategies, underscoring its practical value for real-world deployments that demand seamless integration with rapidly evolving LLM backbones and commercial APIs.

Case Study

In Table
3
, we present a detailed case study from BrowseComp that illustrates the full workflow of MetaAgent. The input task asks for the color of a building that satisfies multiple explicit conditions. While each individual condition may have many candidates, only their intersection leads to the unique correct answer. However, exhaustively enumerating all possibilities for every condition is non-trivial for MetaAgent. Thus, in its initial attempt, MetaAgent retrieves candidates by partially satisfying some conditions and selects a likely answer. Leveraging its self-reflection mechanism, MetaAgent then inspects whether all criteria are actually fulfilled and realizes the chosen answer is incorrect.
Informed by this self-reflection, MetaAgent launches a second attempt, this time systematically checking all constraints for another candidate. Through focused web searches, it identifies that the new candidate fully satisfies the requirements and outputs the correct answer.

Notably, the task input incorporates previously accumulated experience, strategically prompting MetaAgent to “ensure all constraints are satisfied”—a key factor in successful task completion. After solving the case, MetaAgent further reflects on its reasoning process to improve its accumulated task experience, enabling more effective handling of future tasks.
